content: Iodine-129 (129I) is a radioisotope of iodine. It has a half-life of approximately 7 million years and undergoes decay through low-energy beta and gamma emissions, ultimately transforming into xenon-129 (129Xe). Among all fission products, iodine-129 possesses the longest half-life and is one of only seven long-lived fission products. Its fission yield, at 0.6576% per fission, is about 10% of the yield of technetium-99 (99Tc), zirconium-93 (93Zr), or cesium-135 (135Cs), but it is significantly higher than the yield of palladium-107 (107Pd), selenium-79 (79Se), or tin-126 (126Sn). Although larger quantities of heavier iodine isotopes, such as iodine-131 (131I), are produced during fission, these isotopes have short half-lives. As a result, the iodine content in cooled spent nuclear fuel is composed of approximately five-sixths iodine-129 and one-sixth iodine-127, the only stable isotope of iodine. Due to its long half-life, environmental mobility, moderate but sufficient neutron absorption cross-section, and relative lack of dilution by other isotopes of iodine, iodine-129 is considered a leading candidate for disposal through nuclear transmutation. This process involves re-irradiation with neutrons. Technetium-99 (99Tc) is another prominent candidate for this method of disposal among fission products. In contrast, actinide wastes, which are not fission products, are better suited for disposal through fission in fast reactors, accelerator-driven subcritical reactors, or fusion-fission hybrid reactors.
